explanations.explanation: John doesn't hedge. He openly declares, “I am not the Christ.” (John 1:20) Some folks answer a simple question with a ten-minute speech, but John gives it to them straight and plain.

That's the one thing John says he is NOT. The text says he did not refuse to confess, but openly declared, “I am not the Christ.” (John 1:20) The priests and Levites asked who he was, and John made sure they heard that part clearly.

explanations.answer: I am a king of Israel
explanations.explanation: John never claims a crown in this passage. When he's asked who he is, he says, “I am not the Christ.” (John 1:20) Later he describes himself as “a voice of one calling in the wilderness” (John 1:23). A voice is a long way from a throne.
They ask, “Are you the Prophet?” and John answers, “No.” (John 1:21) Notice how short that is. He's had a lot of practice saying no by this point, and he's getting quicker at it.

The text says John does answer no. The visitors ask, “Are you the Prophet?” and he answers, “No.” (John 1:21) He's not unsure and he's not dodging. It's just a plain no, one more name he says he doesn't own.

explanations.answer: With the words of a prophet
explanations.explanation: John replies “in the words of Isaiah the prophet.” (John 1:23) Isaiah was a prophet who spoke for God long before John's day. So John doesn't use his own words to describe himself. He borrows words that were already written down.

explanations.answer: With the name of his family
explanations.explanation: John never gives a family name here. The visitors need an answer for those who sent them, and John replies “in the words of Isaiah the prophet.” (John 1:23) Isaiah was a prophet who spoke for God. If they came for a name for the paperwork, they left with something else.
No miracle shows up in this answer. John simply speaks, “in the words of Isaiah the prophet.” (John 1:23) Isaiah was a prophet who spoke for God. The whole answer is words, and they're enough.
The voice calls, “Make straight the way for the Lord.” (John 1:23) That is the message John says he is carrying. He's not the destination. He's the one shouting that somebody important is on the way.
No walls in this one. The voice in the wilderness calls, “Make straight the way for the Lord.” (John 1:23) Straight walls would be a fine thing for a builder, but that's not what this call is about.
Nice straight rows would make a farmer proud, but that's not the call. The voice says, “Make straight the way for the Lord.” (John 1:23) The straightening is for the Lord's way.

The Pharisees ask, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” (John 1:25) Baptizing is what John is out there doing. They counted up the things he said he's not, and then asked about what he IS doing.

Their question isn't about fasting. They ask, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” (John 1:25) The word is baptize, the thing John was doing at the Jordan.

Praying isn't what they bring up. The Pharisees ask, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” (John 1:25) Their puzzle is about baptizing. I think they wanted to know what gave him the right to do it.

John says, “among you stands One you do not know.” (John 1:26) Think about that. This One is standing right there in the crowd, and they don't know Him. John is pointing at something they walked right past.
Trust isn't the word John uses. He says, “among you stands One you do not know.” (John 1:26) It's about not knowing Him. The text doesn't say they distrust Him, only that they don't know Him.
John doesn't talk about fear here. He says, “among you stands One you do not know.” (John 1:26) The missing piece is knowing Him. Nobody in the text is described as afraid of Him.

explanations.answer: He is far greater than John
explanations.explanation: John says he's not worthy to untie the straps of this One's sandals. (John 1:27) The straps are about as low a job as you could name, and John says even that is above him. I think that tells you how high John sees this One.

explanations.answer: He is a servant like John
explanations.explanation: John puts himself far below this One, not beside Him. He says he isn't worthy to untie the straps of His sandals. (John 1:27) Nobody lines up next to someone like that. They stand back.

explanations.answer: He has traveled a long way
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about a long trip. John says he isn't worthy to untie the straps of this One's sandals. (John 1:27) The point is who this One is, not how far His sandals have walked.

John says, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) Notice how big that is. Not one town's sin or one person's, but the sin of the world. And John points straight at Jesus when he says it.
That's not what John says the Lamb takes away. His words are, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) He names sin, and he names the whole world.
John doesn't mention the sick here. He says, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) The Lamb takes away sin, and not just in one place but in the world.

John says, “A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.” (John 1:30) It sounds like a riddle, since He comes after John yet was before him. John says it plainly, and I'll let the words sit there.
The text says it is true. John says, “A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.” (John 1:30) The reason he gives is that Jesus was before him.

John says, “the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.” (John 1:31) So John's baptizing has a purpose behind it. He's the one pulling back the curtain so Israel can see Jesus.
No crown in this verse. John says, “the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.” (John 1:31) The word is revealed, as in shown to Israel.
Promised isn't John's word. He says, “the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.” (John 1:31) It's about Jesus being revealed, made known to Israel.

John doesn't say the Spirit went back up. He says he saw the Spirit “descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.” (John 1:32) The Spirit came down and rested, and that's where John leaves it.

John says the Spirit came down and rested. He saw the Spirit “descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.” (John 1:32) Then in verse 33 he mentions the Spirit descending and resting on the man. Nothing about going back up.

The One who sent John told him the man with the Spirit resting on Him “is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.” (John 1:33) John baptizes with water, and this man baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Same word, very different gift.
Living water isn't in this verse. John was told the man on whom he sees the Spirit rest “is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.” (John 1:33) That's the thing this man baptizes with.
John isn't told anything about oil. The One who sent him said the man he sees the Spirit rest on “is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.” (John 1:33) So the answer is the Holy Spirit.
John says, “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.” (John 1:34) He saw the sign with his own eyes. Then he said it out loud for everyone to hear.
John doesn't call Jesus that. He says, “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.” (John 1:34) Son of God is the title John gives Him.
John never says that about Jesus here. His testimony is, “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.” (John 1:34) He calls Jesus the Son of God, which is a title for who He is.
